notes.1: Some candidates only read as far as ‘average’ and immediately calculated the average of the three times for 10 swings. If they had read further, they would have found ‘one’ emboldened, emphasising that they were expected to divide that ten-swing time by ten.
notes.2: Almost all candidates recognised that the right-hand portion of the table indicated a constant speed, but only stronger candidates knew that the increasing speed on the left-hand side indicated acceleration.
notes.3: Nearly all candidates recognised the units of mass and weight, but fewer candidates knew that the conversion factor is 10 N / kg rather than 10 N / g. Cambridge International General Certificate of Secondary Education 0625 Physics November 2022
notes.5: The moment of a force is found by multiplying the force by its (perpendicular) distance from the fulcrum. Increasing either will increase the moment. Most candidates knew that you had to increase at least one, but a minority realised that you could do it by increasing either.
notes.6: If the object is moving at a constant speed there is no acceleration, and therefore no resultant force. The only diagram showing a resultant force of zero is A , which only the strongest candidates chose. B and D , which were the most popular choices have resultant forcers of 2 N to the right and 1 N to the right respectively.
notes.9: The most popular response was D , that nuclear power stations release large quantities of carbon dioxide. Nuclear power may have many disadvantages, but the overwhelming point in its favour is precisely that it doesn’t release carbon dioxide.
notes.11: Weaker candidates often thought that the area of a pond affects the pressure at the bottom, whereas stronger candidates recognised that only the depth and density matter. Pascal’s vases is a well-known apparatus to demonstrate this fact.
notes.14: Many candidates chose A , perhaps imagining that the scale divisions on a liquid-in-glass thermometer that have numbers printed by them (typically at 10°C, 20°C, 30°C, etc.) are the fixed points.
notes.17: Syllabus statement 2.3.2 is quite specific in relating convection to density changes. However, many candidates chose one of the distractors.
notes.18: When answering this kind of question, candidates should tick correct statements and to put crosses by incorrect statements. Only then, when they have dealt with the physics, should they consider the logic of the responses, deciding which response matches their pattern of ticks and crosses.
notes.20: Most candidates thought that the image lies in the plane of the mirror and only a minority recognised that it lies as far behind the mirror as the object is in front.
notes.21: Option B was commonly selected by the weakest candidates but was incorrect.
notes.22: The key to this question was to know the regions of the electromagnetic spectrum in order, and so to identify S as visible light. A further clue was provided by it being the only region with a very narrow range of wavelengths. A common misconception was to suppose that mobile phones use radio waves rather than the microwaves that are explicitly stated in section 3.3 of the syllabus.
notes.23: Only the strongest candidates were aware that all electromagnetic waves have the same speed in vacuo. Cambridge International General Certificate of Secondary Education 0625 Physics November 2022
notes.26: The most reliable way to answer this type of question is to evaluate all three currents, writing their values next to the table, thereby dealing with the physics. Then candidates should look at the logic of the options, taking great care to work from smallest to largest (in this case) rather than the other way round.
notes.27: There was evidence of guesswork here from the weaker candidates. Syllabus section 4.2.3 is explicit about the answer.
notes.29: Stronger candidates were able to answer this correctly.
notes.30: Section 4.3.3 of the syllabus asks candidates to describe the action of a variable potential divider. However, many candidates thought that an increased p.d. across the lamp would result in less brightness or vice versa (options B and C ).
notes.31: Many candidates were able to answer this correctly.
notes.32: Despite the similarity between the circuit symbols for a buzzer and a bell, many candidates made the right choice and answered correctly.
notes.33: There is a difference between preventing a short circuit and protecting against the consequences of a short circuit, so option B was incorrect. Fuses generally prevent too high a current in the next stretch of cable, so option D was the right answer.
notes.35: Candidates should be familiar with the right-hand grip rule: that if you grip a straight conductor in the right hand with the thumb indicating the direction of conventional current, then the fingers will indicate the direction of the surrounding magnetic field. Not all candidates knew this.
notes.36: Stronger candidates were successful here, while weaker candidates appeared to guess.
notes.38: Even quite strong candidates chose the lead screen, which would be pointless since the alpha particles will be absorbed by the air long before they reach it. The correct answer is to use tongs since they will prevent the hand penetrating the danger zone within 3 cm or so of the source. Keeping a good distance away from a radioactive source is always the best protection.
notes.39: Only the strongest candidates were able to deal with this graphical analysis. Cambridge International General Certificate of Secondary Education 0625 Physics November 2022
